https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-p.text: Ukraine has intelligence that Russia is planning new ground offensives against Kyiv and Chernihiv — while Moscow ramps up drone strikes on Ukrainian cities. Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told reporters that Russian military chiefs have been tasked by the Kremlin’s political leaders with planning and preparing for attacks on the two cities, according to intelligence received and verified by Ukraine. Palisa said there is not yet evidence that Russian troops are gathering to carry out the attacks, and that Ukraine’s priority is to “prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to launch any offensive actions at all.” Advertisement Advertisement Russian forces previously attempted a ground attack on Kyiv at the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, launched in part from nearby Belarus, but were ultimately repelled by the Ukrainian military. Palisa's comments come not long after a Wall Street Journal report that Russia is testing its ability to mobilize more troops. The Kremlin is now losing more troops than it can recruit, while a growing exodus of Russians reflects escalating fears that Moscow is poised to announce a new mobilization effort. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Saturday that “escalation from Russia's side is progressing.” He made those comments following a briefing from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unexpected visit to Moscow, where he warned Russian officials not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies. Ukraine needs more air support, Tusk said, adding that the next six months “will be decisive, and we must be prepared as Poland and NATO for various scenarios.” Russia is bombarding Kyiv with “virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday . In a separate video address Friday evening, he admitted Ukraine needs to “significantly accelerate” production of interceptors capable of taking down Iranian-designed Shahed drones.

(Russ Dillingham/Staff Photographer) Improvements to heating and air ventilation at Minot Consolidated School are “pretty much complete,” Regional School Unit 16 Superintendent Amy Hediger said. The school board in January approved a tax-exempt lease purchase of $2.82 million to make heating and ventilation improvements at the school, with the expectation that work would begin this summer. Changes made over the summer included all-new ventilation, new ductwork and a new control system for heating and ventilation, Hediger said in an email. Also, a new burner was added to the school’s boiler that allows them to switch from heating oil and propane to help control fuel costs. All that’s left to do, Hediger said, is to complete air quality testing and set up the system for accessing real-time information. Valves and motors that were no longer functioning were replaced as well, Hediger said. “This project is probably 97% complete,” she said. Advertisement Voters in Mechanic Falls, Minot in Poland approved a $6 million state loan in June. The loan will fund work on the ventilation and HVAC systems at Poland Regional High School, Bruce Whittier Middle School and Poland Community School, all in Poland, and Elm Street School in Mechanic Falls. District voters had rejected similar loans in the past. Related Poland parents raise concerns over air quality in classrooms In April, some parents of students in RSU 16 said their kids had experienced health problems related to elevated levels of carbon dioxide in the classrooms. In response, Hediger ordered the district to place CO2 monitors throughout the schools. https://londonlovesbusiness.com/russia-t.text: Tech Property Business London Loves Image: X Business News Defence Politics News World News Russia threatens ‘necessary measures’ as Lithuania prepares NATO build-up by Mark Channer Chief Defence and Security Editor October 7, 2026 written by Mark Channer Chief Defence and Security Editor 7 th Oct 26 12:16 pm Lithuania’s decision to consider removing its constitutional prohibition on nuclear weapons and offer to finance a permanent US military base has triggered a sharp warning from Moscow, exposing the growing risks of military escalation along NATO’s eastern flank. The Kremlin said the moves represented a significant deterioration in the security environment around Russia, as Vilnius seeks deeper American military involvement to deter potential aggression. Dmitry Peskov, Vladimir Putin’s spokesman, warned that Moscow would be “forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security” if NATO military capabilities continued to expand close to Russian territory. “A build-up of NATO forces on Russia’s doorstep cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions , just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighbouring country cannot,” Peskov said. “This marks yet another significant escalation of tensions.” The confrontation centres on two developments in Lithuania. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has confirmed that Vilnius is prepared to fund a dedicated American military facility, shortly after Donald Trump said Washington would “certainly look” at establishing a permanent US presence in the Baltic state. Read more related news: Expert fears UK and Europe ‘will wake up only after capitals are hit’ then ‘it’s too late’ Zelensky issues chilling warning as Ukraine rushes to defend cities Labour is playing with British lives as Burnham leaves defence dangerously underfunded Two dead and almost 200 isolated as mystery plague spreads in Russia Lithuania’s parliament has also advanced a constitutional amendment that would remove the country’s longstanding prohibition on hosting weapons of mass destruction. A final vote is scheduled for January. If approved, the change would remove a legal barrier to the possible deployment of NATO nuclear weapons on Lithuanian territory, although no decision has been announced to station US nuclear weapons there. The geographic implications are nevertheless stark. Lithuania borders Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave and sits alongside Belarus, Moscow’s closest military ally in the region. Lithuania does not possess its own nuclear arsenal. Several European NATO members already participate in arrangements under which US nuclear weapons are stationed on their territory while remaining under American control. For Vilnius, the issue is less about acquiring nuclear weapons than strengthening deterrence. Around 1,000 US troops are already stationed in Lithuania on a rotational basis, alongside American Abrams tanks and other armoured forces. Germany is also preparing to establish a permanent brigade of about 5,000 troops in the country by the end of next year . Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas welcomed Trump’s comments on a permanent American presence, saying they showed the US president “knows Lithuania, knows our investments, knows our determination to build security and appreciates it.” Lithuania has increasingly positioned itself as one of Europe’s most heavily armed frontline states. Defence spending is expected to reach 5.38 per cent of gross domestic product this year, reflecting the perceived threat from Russia and the country’s proximity to Kaliningrad and Belarus. The military build-up comes against an increasingly volatile backdrop. The Baltic region has experienced a series of airspace incidents, including a drone crossing from Belarus that was shot down by Italian fighter jets and reported incursions by Russian aircraft. The latest dispute also follows a warning from Putin over Kaliningrad. Russian officials have threatened to deploy nuclear weapons if NATO attempts to attack or blockade the Russian exclave, an isolated but heavily militarised territory between Poland and Lithuania. Russian officials in London have separately warned against British media simulations of a potential Baltic conflict, telling those contemplating action against Kaliningrad to “have no illusions about the consequences.” The danger is not that Lithuania’s constitutional change automatically produces a nuclear deployment. It is that each side increasingly interprets the other’s defensive preparations as evidence of offensive intent. That dynamic is reshaping the Baltic security environment: more troops produce demands for more deterrence, which prompts Moscow to threaten countermeasures, which in turn strengthens the argument for further NATO reinforcement. For Europe, the central risk is that this cycle continues without either side deliberately choosing a wider confrontation. But with American forces, German troops and potentially a new legal framework for nuclear weapons converging on a state bordering Russia’s most militarised Baltic territory, the margin for miscalculation is becoming increasingly narrow. https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-c.text: BRUSSELS — European coffin manufacturers are joining forces to ask Brussels to investigate Chinese imports, warning that low prices and potential customs loopholes are threatening an industry built around one of the continent’s most predictable markets: death. A group of manufacturers — which until now had no dedicated lobby representation — has formed a coalition and met with European Commission officials, including from its trade department, the initiative’s organizers told POLITICO. The group is preparing an anti-dumping complaint — a request for the EU to investigate whether Chinese coffin makers are selling their products in Europe at unfairly low prices. The industry says the damage is already being felt. Over the past five years roughly a quarter of European coffin manufacturers have shut down, their numbers falling from about 120 to 90, according to Folco Ciulli, a consultant helping coordinate the complaint. Advertisement Advertisement “Smaller companies were unable to withstand competition from non-European importers,” Ciulli said, adding those that survived have absorbed only half the production previously handled by the businesses that closed. The push follows an appeal by a group of EU lawmakers to Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič last year. The MEPs raised concerns about Chinese competition, and were told the industry could submit a formal trade complaint . “The EU takes robust action to protect its industries from unfairly traded imports and at present has over 200 measures in place,” a Commission spokesperson said. They declined to confirm meetings with the manufacturers, saying contacts with industry over potential trade defense complaints are confidential. The price of death At the heart of the industry’s case is a stark price difference. According to manufacturers’ estimates, producing a coffin in China costs roughly one-third as much as an equivalent product in Italy, even when the same type of wood is used. The coalition — which has yet to agree on a name for itself — flags several factors it believes give Chinese producers an advantage, including state subsidies, export-related tax benefits, lower labor costs and cheaper timber. It also argues that Chinese manufacturers benefit from preferential raw-material supply chains, and that higher U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods have helped redirect production toward Europe. Advertisement Advertisement But cheap prices alone don’t constitute dumping under EU trade rules. To secure anti-dumping duties, European manufacturers must provide evidence that Chinese producers are selling coffins in the EU below their established normal value, that the EU industry is suffering material injury, and that dumped imports are responsible for that injury. The coalition is therefore collecting detailed information on production costs, raw materials, labor and factory-gate prices to compare equivalent coffins manufactured in China and Europe. Not adding up? European coffin manufacturers are also examining a hypothesis that some coffins entering the EU from China are not being categorized as such by customs authorities. Emiliano Inguscio, a mathematician hired by the industry to analyze trade and production data, said his calculations had identified an unexplained discrepancy equivalent to around 30,000 coffins a year in Italy. “In theory, the number of coffins available for consumption should broadly correspond to domestic production plus imports, minus exports and adjusted for changes in inventories,” Inguscio explained. Advertisement Advertisement Because demand for coffins is relatively predictable and closely linked to mortality, he argues, significant discrepancies could indicate that some imports are not being properly recorded. The coalition is concerned that such shipments could escape accurate recording in import statistics, obscuring the true extent of Chinese competition. This has led to a hypothesis that manufacturers have dubbed the “IKEA loophole,” by which some Chinese coffins arrive in Europe flat-packed, with their components declared to customs as wooden parts rather than finished funeral products. Once inside the EU, the pieces are assembled and sold as coffins, the theory goes. The Commission confirmed that unassembled goods can still be classified as finished products under international customs rules, provided they retain the essential characteristics of the completed item. That means a flat-packed coffin cannot necessarily be treated simply as wooden components for customs purposes. The industry has also raised a second hypothetical loophole: coffins being imported as packaging for other merchandise, rather than declared as commercial products in their own right. A widening trade battle The coffin-makers’ campaign reflects a broader shift in Europe’s trade disputes with China, as complaints about low-cost competition spread beyond strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, steel and chemicals to more traditional manufactured goods. Advertisement Advertisement According to the Commission’s latest annual trade defense report , published in September, the EU launched 32 new trade defense investigations in 2025, nearly matching the previous year’s record. Coffin-makers would not be the first relatively small, traditional European industry to win protection. In January, the Commission imposed anti-dumping duties of between 56% and 60% on Chinese candles following an investigation into damage to an EU industry employing around 9,000 people across 80 companies.
